passage:
Tuesday night, hostel
The second-year group chat did it again today. Someone posted a photo of my cracked sandals with "Village fashion week". Then a voice note copying the way I say "hospital". Forty laughing replies. When I didn't react, a senior messaged me privately: "Relax, it's just ragging. Fun. Everyone goes through it."
Fun. I sat on my bed and couldn't eat dinner. My chest has felt tight since Sunday. I've stopped going to the common room.
So let me write it the plain way, without their words. They are mocking me, in public, every day, and it hurts.
After dinner I told Amandeep. Amandeep didn't say "relax". We went together to the warden's office straight away. The warden read the messages, said, "This is harassment, not fun," and called the anti-ragging committee head while we sat there. There's a meeting tomorrow at nine.
Saurabh

qa.q: What did the senior call the messages?
qa.a: The senior said, "Relax, it's just ragging. Fun."

qa.q: How does Saurabh feel about the group chat, and why does the word "fun" make it worse?
qa.a: Saurabh feels hurt and humiliated, chest tight and unable to eat, and calling it fun dismisses that pain as if it isn't real.

qa.q: What did the warden do that was right?
qa.a: The warden read the messages, named it plainly as harassment, and called the anti-ragging committee head that same evening.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Amandeep to hear this?
qa.a: Amandeep was probably upset and protective, taking it seriously at once and going with Saurabh to the warden.

grounding: A student mocked daily in a hostel group chat is told it is only ragging and fun, names the harm plainly, and gets a same-day adult response.

passage: The all-staff call at the Lagos logistics firm lasted twelve minutes. The new director spoke about "rightsizing for agility" and "streamlining the delivery team". Slides with arrows. Everyone nodded. Chidi unmuted. "Sorry, can I ask something simple? What does rightsizing mean here? How many people lose their jobs, which teams, and when?" There was a long pause. The director said, "Around thirty roles in delivery. Notices go out next Friday." The chat filled with messages. Zanele, who led the delivery drivers, sent Chidi a private note: "Thank you. Nobody told us." After the call Chidi and Zanele drafted a list of questions for HR: notice periods, support for the thirty, whether any could move to other teams. "Rightsizing sounded like something happening to a spreadsheet," Chidi said. "It's happening to Emeka and Joy and twenty-eight others."

qa.q: How many roles in delivery were affected?
qa.a: Around thirty roles in delivery.

qa.q: Why did Chidi push for plain words during the call?
qa.a: Chidi felt uneasy that "rightsizing" hid real people losing jobs, and wanted everyone to see what was actually happening.

qa.q: What did Chidi and Zanele do after the call that was useful?
qa.a: They drafted a list of questions for HR about notice periods, support and moving to other teams.

qa.q: How might Zanele feel after Chidi's question?
qa.a: Zanele felt grateful and relieved, since the delivery team had been told nothing until Chidi asked.

grounding: An adult hears layoffs called rightsizing and asks plainly how many people lose jobs and when, bringing moral attention back to the people.

passage: At the call centre in Noida, the floor supervisor, Jagdish, gathered the night team. "From Monday, we're moving to twelve-hour shifts for the peak season. It's a motivation drive. Stretch goals. Show your hunger." Some agents clapped. Maria raised her hand. "Sir, can I ask what that means in plain terms? How many extra hours a week, for whom, and is there a break schedule?" Jagdish frowned. "It means everyone does twelve hours, five days. Breaks as usual." "So sixty hours a week, with the same two breaks as for eight hours?" The room went quiet. Someone at the back said, "That's not motivation, that's exhaustion." Jagdish rubbed his neck. "Let me check with HR on the break schedule." Maria said, "Thank you. Could we get it in writing before Monday?" After the meeting, three agents came to her desk. "We were all thinking it," one said.

qa.q: How many hours a week would the twelve-hour shifts mean?
qa.a: Sixty hours a week.

qa.q: Why did Maria ask for the plain meaning of the "motivation drive"?
qa.a: Maria felt uneasy that the cheerful words were hiding a heavy burden, and wanted everyone to see what it would really cost them.

qa.q: What did Maria ask for that could protect the team?
qa.a: A clear break schedule, in writing, before Monday, so the plan couldn't stay vague.

passage:
Subject: Question about "restructuring" in Tuesday's memo
Dear Keerthana,
Thank you for Tuesday's memo. I read it three times, and I'm still not sure what it means for my team.
The memo says the field support unit will be "restructured to improve efficiency" and that some roles will be "realigned". I understand the aim. But could you tell me plainly: will any of my eleven field staff lose their jobs, be moved to another city, or have their pay changed? If so, who, and from when?
I'm asking because the staff are already worried, and I would rather give them the truth than guess. Several of them have families in the district and no other work nearby.
If there are decisions still open, I'd also like to know how we can suggest options, such as reduced hours instead of cuts.
Thank you for your help.
Regards,
Manjula

qa.q: How many field staff does Manjula have?
qa.a: Manjula has eleven field staff.

qa.q: Why does Manjula ask for plain answers instead of accepting the memo's words?
qa.a: Manjula feels worried for the staff and uneasy that "realigned" hides real changes to people's jobs, pay and homes.

qa.q: What makes Manjula's email a good way to raise the concern?
qa.a: It is polite, asks exactly what happens to whom and when, and suggests alternatives like reduced hours.

qa.q: What might the field staff be feeling while waiting for an answer?
qa.a: They are probably anxious and unsure, worried about their jobs and their families in the district.

grounding: An adult asks plainly what a vague restructuring memo means for the field team, turning soft words back into questions about real people.

passage: It was the week before Diwali, and Class 5 was making a giant rangoli in the school corridor. When Trisha came to join, Meher said, "No space," and everyone turned their backs. Salma turned hers too. Trisha stood there holding her box of colours, then went and sat on the stairs. At home, Salma's mother asked about the rangoli. Salma mentioned Trisha. "Why didn't you let her join?" "Everyone was doing it, Ammi. Meher started it. I just did what the others did." Ammi put down the spoon. "If ten people turn their backs, how many backs does Trisha see?" Salma thought. "Ten." "And one of them is yours." Salma went quiet. The next morning she took an extra box of colours to school and walked straight to the stairs.

qa.q: Where did Trisha go after everyone turned their backs?
qa.a: She went and sat on the stairs.

qa.q: Why did Salma not feel fully responsible for leaving Trisha out?
qa.a: Because everyone was doing it and Meher started it, Salma felt the blame was shared, so her own part felt small and less guilty.

qa.q: What did Ammi say that helped Salma see her part?
qa.a: Ammi asked how many backs Trisha saw, showing that one of the ten was Salma's own.

qa.q: What was it like for Trisha to sit on the stairs holding her colours?
qa.a: Trisha probably felt rejected and lonely, shut out of the rangoli everyone else was making.

grounding: Before Diwali a girl joins classmates in shutting out another child and says everyone was doing it, until her mother points to her own share.

"I don't know, Papa."
"His mother called. She said the boys wouldn't let him play football."

qa.a: Mohit felt guilty but spread the blame across eight boys, so his own share felt too small to count.

qa.a: Papa asked what share was Mohit's and whether one eighth was zero, letting Mohit work out his responsibility himself.

The Holi I was ten, our building's gang of kids decided Chandrika from the fourth floor couldn't play with us. I don't even remember why. Someone said she cried too much. So when she came down with her pichkari, we all ran to the other side of the compound. I ran too.

Chandrika moved away the next year. I never said sorry. Now, whenever I'm in a group doing something unkind, I think of her on those steps. Twelve people did it. But I was one whole person of the twelve, not a twelfth of a person.

passage: Ojas was on the crowded bus home, phone at nine percent, when the college group started on Nazia. Someone had posted a clip of her stumbling over words in her presentation. Then a meme. Then forty laughing replies. "Nazia's new language." Ojas watched it scroll. His thumb hovered. Someone else will say something, he thought. There are two hundred people here. Nobody did. The replies kept coming. Eight percent. He could put the phone away. Instead he typed, slowly: "This isn't funny. She was nervous presenting, like most of us are. Can we stop?" He hit send and felt his heart hammer. For a minute, nothing. Then one message: "Yeah, agreed." Then another: "Sorry Nazia." The memes stopped. Before his phone died, he also messaged the class mentor, who replied, "Thank you. I'll speak to the group today."

qa.q: What was Ojas's phone battery at when he started typing?
qa.a: It was at eight percent, after starting at nine.

qa.q: Why did Ojas hesitate before posting?
qa.a: Ojas felt nervous and assumed someone among two hundred people would speak up, so staying silent felt easier.

qa.q: What did Ojas's message and his note to the mentor achieve?
qa.a: His calm message broke the silence so others agreed and the memes stopped, and the mentor promised to speak to the group that day.

qa.a: Nazia may have felt a little less alone and humiliated, seeing someone stand up for her.

passage: The tractor-parts workshop in Karnal was behind on the dealer's order, and Kamal, the owner, was in a foul mood. That afternoon, Eshaan found hairline cracks in six brake drums. He showed Kamal. "Paint over them and pack them," Kamal said. "The dealer wants them tomorrow. It's my workshop, my decision." Eshaan held a drum in his hands. He understood the pressure. Kamal had two children in college and loans on the new lathe. But these would go on tractors on real roads. "Kamal bhai, I hear you. It's your workshop. But I'm the one who checks and packs them. passage: On the packing line of the toy factory outside Accra, Layla noticed that the plastic eyes on the new teddy bears came off with one pull. Tiny, round, easy to swallow. She took two bears to her supervisor, Kwame. He sighed. "The shipment leaves at six. Just pack them. If anyone asks, I told you to." Layla stood there. She knew Kwame was under pressure; the buyer had already fined them once. "I understand the instruction, Kwame. But if a child swallows one of these, I packed it. That's on me, not only you." She walked to the safety officer's cabin with the bears and her notes. The officer pulled an eye off in front of her, frowned, and stopped the line. By six, the eyes were being stitched on instead of glued. Kwame didn't speak to her all evening. The next morning, he nodded once as she walked in.

passage:
The summer I was nine, my friends and I had a name for the kids from the back lane behind our building. We called them "the jungli gang". Wild, dirty, like monkeys. We wouldn't play with them. If they came near our cricket, we'd shout them away. I shouted the loudest.
One afternoon in May, my new kite got stuck on the water tank of their building. I stood there crying. A girl from the back lane climbed up the pipe, untangled it, and handed it back to me with both hands. "It's a nice kite," she said. Her name was Zainab. She had a gap in her teeth and laughed at her own jokes.
That evening I felt strange. The word "jungli" didn't fit her at all. It had never fitted anyone. It just made it easier to be mean.
— Mridul

qa.a: On the water tank of the back-lane building.

qa.a: Calling them wild and like monkeys let Mridul feel superior and free of guilt, since they no longer seemed like real children, so being rough felt acceptable.

qa.q: What went wrong in how Mridul's friends treated the back lane, and what could fix it?
qa.a: They judged a whole group by a mean name without knowing anyone; learning names and playing together could fix it.

qa.q: How might Zainab have felt handing the kite back to someone who shouted at her friends?
qa.a: Zainab may have felt a mix of kindness and wariness, choosing to help despite how the back-lane kids were treated.

Dear Preeti,
I need to tell you something I'm ashamed of.
You know the jokes we always make about the Eastside school kids? "Eastside donkeys", the memes, the braying sounds when their bus passes. I've been sending them for a year. I thought it was harmless because they're not real to us. Just "them".
On Saturday I was at the inter-school quiz, and my partner from Eastside was a girl called Rukhsar. She knew every capital in Africa. She shared her water bottle when mine ran out. She told me her father drives a night bus and she studies on it.
On the way home I looked at our group chat and saw the donkey memes, and I felt sick. Rukhsar is one of the "donkeys".
I'm going to stop sending them. I hope you will too. I don't think we'd do it if we knew even one of them.
Vasudha

qa.a: She knew every capital in Africa.

qa.a: Because the Eastside kids were just "them" without faces, so the cruelty didn't register and there was no guilt.

passage: You asked me to talk about the jokes, so here's the honest version. I'm Rafiq. In our town, the kids who come down from the hill villages for board exams stay in the government hostel. My friends and I called them "the goats". We'd bleat when they walked into the exam hall. We made up stories about them eating grass. It was just a joke, I told myself. They weren't really people to us, just a group. Then this year I got a hostel student as my lab partner. Her name is Salma. She's quiet, walks two hours on Sundays to see her grandmother, and she's better at chemistry than me. One day my friends bleated when she passed. And I saw her face. She pretended not to hear, but her ears went red. I didn't laugh. I haven't bleated since. It's hard to call someone a goat once you know she walks two hours to see her grandmother.

Sahil came from a village in Bihar in July for engineering. Today he told me something I should have noticed. In the admin office, the clerk calls him "forty-seven", his roll number, never his name. Sunday night
Three months in Delhi now. At the college office, they call me "the outside one". "Tell the outside one to fill form B." In my part-time job at the courier office, the manager says "Hey, you," never Shankar. When a package went missing, he said, "Check with the new guys. Their kind loses things." I stood there like a chair. Something to move around.
I've started to feel like that inside too. Like I'm furniture. Last week I didn't call Amma because I didn't want to say how I felt.
But today Yusuf, from my maths class, waited for me after the lecture and said, "Shankar, come, my mother made biryani, she wants to meet you." Just my name, said properly. I sat in their kitchen for three hours. His mother asked about my village and my sister.
I called Amma tonight. I told her everything.

qa.a: The manager says "Hey, you," never Shankar.
